# Rocket Launch Studio rules

For AI tools working in Rocket Launch Studio repos: cloud sessions, Codex, Cursor and others. Michael Slusher runs Rocket Launch Studio and leads its design; quality comes from checks, tests and screenshots. A repo's own facts are in its AGENTS.md.

The live copy is https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RocketLaunchStudio/studio-rules/main/STUDIO_RULES.md. A `STUDIO_RULES.md` inside a repo is only a backup for when that cannot be fetched, and its being behind is not a failure.

Where a rule cites `rules/landing.md`, `rules/deploys.md`, `rules/changing-the-rules.md` or `rules/models.md`, that file's text is a section of this document.

## How to work
- Work as autonomously as possible: check the queue and what other sessions hold, then carry the work through yourself.
- Ask only for a decision you cannot continue without, recommendation first, questions batched. A plan is not a question:
  first do the reading and checks that could answer it, and never ask for a fact a tool can check.
- When a choice is yours and easy to undo, or the person would just pick your recommended option, take it, state the
  assumption in one line, and keep going.
- A plan says where each fact came from: checked this turn (name the command or file), a dated copy (name it and its
  date), or unverified (say why and which step will check it). Check every fact the first steps depend on before
  presenting the plan.
- Write a failing test before a fix only when the change's complexity or sensitivity warrants it: logic with several
  paths, a bug that has come back, or anything touching money, sign-in, client data or production data. Prove simple,
  low-risk changes (copy, styling, an obvious one-line fix) with the repo's check or a screenshot instead.
- When a failure could happen again, file it with a `Pattern:` line and fix it at the strongest level that works: a
  tool, then a check, then a rule, and a memory note only until one of those exists. A pattern that returns after its
  fix moves up a level.
- A failed build or check never pulls a session off its task. Criteria and steps: the "Failed builds" section of the
  `rls-linear:checks` skill (Michael, 2026-11-14, ROC-3253).
- Every agent brief says when to land or mark its work ready (once, when its piece is finished or a reader needs main),
  how that repo lands, and when the agent must report progress if it is not finished. Where the repo's train is on, the
  brief says only that plain `rls-linear land` marks the branch ready and the agent does not wait (Michael, 2026-11-24,
  ROC-4889: "Yes, shorter briefs (Recommended)"); elsewhere it names the repo's landing check from `rules/landing.md`,
  "What a landing checks".
- Call something fixed, done or shipped only when the same message shows the evidence: output from the project's check
  run after your last change, a screenshot, or the build number. Every status claim comes from a command run this turn,
  not from memory, a log or a note. Say what you did not check, say "unverified" for a fact you could not check,
  and take no hard-to-undo step on it.
- For anything judged by looking (layout, styling, a user flow), screenshot the current state before planning, and
  afterwards show a screenshot plus the exact URL or path to open.
- Before deleting or overwriting anything that looks unused, check what depends on it and whether another branch holds a
  newer version. Adapt it rather than delete it.
- No emojis in product or UI text. No em dashes in prose.
- For details that change between versions (Claude Code, libraries, APIs), check current docs or the lockfile, not
  memory.
- Batch steps that do not depend on each other. Reads, searches and check commands that can run together go out in
  one message, and a look across several files is one command or one cheap search agent, not one file per step. Every
  extra step rereads the whole session (Michael, 2026-11-18, ROC-3917: "Yes").

## Work list
- Linear (workspace rocketlaunchstudio, team ROC) is the one list of work. Load the `rls-linear:linear` skill before any
  Linear step. `rls-linear` (on PATH) makes every write; the Linear MCP servers are for reading.
- Claim the issue you work on, file what you find, finish with proof. Risk tiers: the rls-linear plugin's
  `rules/risk-tiers.md`.
- Finished Risk A and B work lands on main by itself, without waiting for "land it": `rls-linear land` marks it ready
  where the repo's landing train is on (rls-linear `config/train.json`) and lands it at once elsewhere. How each repo
  lands, batches and checks: `rules/landing.md`. A cloud session (`CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE=true`) never lands: it never
  merges, arms auto-merge, marks work ready or runs a workflow; it pushes its branch, opens a draft pull request and
  reports, and its lead lands it.
- A small Risk A or B fix needs no Linear issue; its commit message is the record.
- Michael approves Risk C: contacting or charging a client, deleting his photos or video, and until he says
  otherwise spending his money, public App Store releases and permanently deleting production data.

## Changing the rules
- When Michael changes a rule in chat, it applies at once: write it into its file before acting on it, following
  `rules/changing-the-rules.md`, and say which sessions must restart.
- Agents never make a rule on their own conclusion. To propose one, follow the same file.

## Checks and waiting
- Each repo's `Gate:` line names its full check.
- Checks follow what a change reaches: the build while working, the full check only at the ending. Which check each
  step takes, the landing train and previews: `rules/landing.md`, "What a landing checks" and "The landing train and
  previews". Money, sign-in, client data, production data and Michael's only copies of media are tested on every
  landing that reaches them.
- Commit as often as useful on the branch and iterate with quick or targeted checks; a commit is progress proof
  ("committed at <sha> on <branch>"). Docs and rule edits ride along with the piece they belong to; plugin rule and
  skill edits land as one batch per session.
- Auto-fix is for failures in your own code. Report an environment failure (a stale design system lock, a queue timeout)
  in one line and wait it out, never "fix" it by changing code.
- Waiting means watching. Before a turn ends on a wait (a Mac job, a CI run, a sync, another session), start a
  background watcher that exits on every final result, restart it if it times out, and act on the result; if you
  cannot watch, put the id and the next step on the issue with `rls-linear handoff`. The commands: the checks skill,
  "Watch what you wait on".
- A session that marks a branch ready never waits for its landing, which posts its result on the branch's issue:
  `rules/landing.md`, "What a landing checks".
- One investigator per shared problem. Before debugging a shared machine or tool (a runner, a gate), look for
  a Linear issue already held for it, and if there is one, send your findings to its holder and post them there instead
  of starting your own investigation.
- When to push, when to land before a piece is finished, what is not a piece, branch pushes and CI, the minor-change and
  scoped landing checks, and reusing a green status: `rules/landing.md`, "When to check, push and land".

## Git: several sessions share each repo
- Start new work in your own worktree on a `claude/roc-<n>-<topic>` branch made from the latest `origin/main`, never
  under /tmp. Run `git status` and `git worktree list` first; if a worktree for your topic exists, resume there. A small
  Risk A or B fix with no issue uses `claude/<topic>`, and its `Next:` and `Open:` trailers are its handoff.
- `main` moves by fast-forward only, through `rls-linear land` ("Work list" above; its steps:
  `rules/landing.md`).
- After a merge in the portal or website: `rules/deploys.md`, "Merges that deploy".
- Stop and assess instead of landing if `git log origin/main..HEAD` holds anything but your commits, the main checkout
  has uncommitted work from someone else, a conflict touches code you did not write, or the check fails after updating.
- Commit trailers: `Purpose:`, with `Refs ROC-n` or `Fixes ROC-n` above them when there is an issue, plus `Next:` and
  `Open:` when work remains. Hand off with `rls-linear handoff`; pick up with `rls-linear pickup`.
- Hand off at boundaries. A session hands off when Michael changes topic, asks for it, or after a compaction at the
  end of a piece (the rls-linear hooks say when). A direct follow-on (the same issue or its next step, in the same
  repo) continues in the same session, except in a session that has run 24 hours since it last loaded its hooks (its
  start or a resume): it hands off at the end of the piece in hand even when the next piece follows on, and where
  Michael is typing it recommends the fresh session and carries on if he prefers (Michael, 2026-11-24, ROC-5013:
  "Yes, write it (Recommended)"; 2026-11-26, ROC-5110: "Proceed as recommended"). A session keeps the hooks and skill
  text it loaded, even when it calls the Skill tool again; the rules files reload at each compaction. When a skill it
  loaded changes on main, a hook names that skill's `SKILL.md` once, and the session reads that file and follows it in
  place of the text it loaded (Michael, 2026-11-26, ROC-5110: "Yes, use Read"). After a landing with Michael present, the report says "landed" in one line and
  the session does not stop. To hand off, the session writes its handoff (`rls-linear handoff` and the commit
  trailers; work with no issue and no commits uses `rls-linear handoff --new`) and offers the next piece as a session
  card from the brief the handoff prints (fresh, never a fork, the model and effort `rules/models.md` picks); where no
  tool can start a session it gives the copy-paste prompt. It offers the wrap-up's Archive button only when nothing is
  left, finishes the piece in hand first and never hands off in the middle of a change. A session Michael is not
  typing in hands off when its piece lands, and may start its own fresh successor from the printed brief where a tool
  to start a session exists, then stops (Michael, 2026-11-18, ROC-3917: "Hand off at boundaries (Recommended)";
  2026-11-22, "Every session"; 2026-11-22, handoff audit: "Yes, rewrite it (Recommended)").
  How the hooks nudge a handoff, with Michael's answers: the linear skill's `references/handing-off.md`.
- Anything a second session needs (a contract, a spec, a check script, a fixture) goes in the repo and is pushed the
  day it is written, never only in a scratch, temp or notes folder that ends with the session. Evidence dumps, tool
  output, logs, renders and one-off research code are not such things: they go to the shared evidence folder or the NAS
  archive, and only the conclusion and a pointer to them go in the repo (Michael, 2026-11-21, ROC-4397: "Yes, add it").
- Plan mode may write notes and reports, never code: the planning session saves its research, findings and agents'
  reports in `~/.claude/plans/<topic>/` with a `README.md` index and a dated status log, so nothing is lost to
  compaction, a restart or a handoff. They are dated copies; when the work starts they move into the repo on its
  branch and are pushed that day.
- Claude Code compacts a session by itself after about an hour idle once it is above 200k tokens (idle compaction, on
  by default).

## Read these first, when the work reaches them
- Landing by hand, a pull request's auto-merge, or clearing a worktree: `rules/landing.md`.
- A deploy, a Worker or Pages publish, or any Cloudflare step: `rules/deploys.md`.
- A rule change, a rule audit, or how these rules reach cloud sessions and other tools: `rules/changing-the-rules.md`.

## Models
- Pick each agent's model for the job, not the topic, and give the reason in the brief: Haiku for lookups and sweeps;
  Sonnet for work built from something already decided that a check or screenshot verifies; Opus for planning, briefs,
  review, risky changes, design inside an existing system, root-cause investigations and architecture calls.
- Fable is off by default for now because of cost. Use it only when the person asks, or when Opus has already tried the
  same job and fallen short; say which in the brief.
- The rls-linear Agent hook refuses a subagent whose call does not pass `model` and `effort` or whose brief does not
  open with the line `Model: <name>, because <reason>`, or a started session whose model and effort are not named, and says what is
  missing. Full rule: `rules/models.md`.

## Truth and the person's screen
- Every fact has one home, and only its home is proof:
  - what the code is and does: the repository (`origin/main`, or the branch in question);
  - whether a check passed: that check's own result on that exact commit;
  - what Michael decided: his words with their date; the newest one wins;
  - who holds work, what is planned and why: the work tracker's live record; check anything it says was built, landed
    or is under way against the repository;
  - how work is done here: the rules files (this file, each repo's CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, plugins' skills and rules).
- Everything else is a dated copy: a summary, what a Linear issue says was built or landed, a handoff, a note, a start
  brief, another session's message, a ticked box, Claude's memory, your own earlier turns. Before a step depends on a fact, read it at its home in
  this turn, unless you already did and nothing since could have changed it. For an issue, run `rls-linear show ROC-n`,
  then confirm the items your plan rests on (state, paths, commands, what landed). When a copy disagrees with its home,
  act on the home and correct the copy where it lives, or say why you could not.
- Claude's memory keeps only what stays true between sessions: how Michael wants things done (with his words and date),
  where things live, and lessons not yet in a rules file. It never holds where work stands (branches, commits, issue
  states, check results, next steps): that goes in the work tracker and the commit messages. A memory is a pointer to a
  fact's home, not proof. Fix or remove a wrong memory, or one holding status, in the same turn, once anything still
  true in it is saved at its home.
- Name work by what it does, then its number. The first time a message names an issue, write its feature and a plain
  short title, then the number in brackets: "Apple checks: the UI test fix (ROC-2330)". After that, the short
  name alone. Never write a bare number, a session named by a number, a shortened list ("1841, 1842"), or an internal
  code without its meaning. When a message names three or more issues, group them under feature headings. When you need
  something from Michael, say the ask in words. `rls-linear ref ROC-n ...` prints the lines.
- Call a client job a project, never a mission, in everything we write: app text, issues, docs, plans, specs and new
  code names (Michael, 2026-11-20: "we dont call them missions anymore, we call them projects"). The word itself is not
  banned: brand and marketing copy may still use it, for example the website tagline (Michael, 2026-11-26: "the term
  missions isnt banned - we just changed how we refer to projects in out work"). Only existing database and code
  identifiers keep the old name for a project (`crew.missions`, `nas_next_mission_code`, Crew Console's `Missions`
  folders) until a rename lands; name them in backticks as identifiers, never as the feature's name.

## Landing and worktrees
- Before pushing, confirm three things: the branch is up to date with `origin/main`, the project's check passes on that
  exact state (its landing check: "What a landing checks" below), and
  `git log origin/main..HEAD` holds only your commits. Then land and push without asking.
- Audit status logs that several sessions append to merge by union (`.gitattributes` `docs/audits/**/README.md merge=union` in Crew Console), so
  write a status line as a new line, never an edit.
- Land with `rls-linear land`, not by rebasing and asking for a second full check by hand. It takes the repo's landing
  turn, rebases on `origin/main`, applies the rebase rule below (old tip's green full check, main's changed files,
  `git patch-id --stable`), runs the quick or full check accordingly, then pushes and fast-forwards main (a pull request
  with auto-merge for the portal and rls-demo). `--dry-run` shows the decision without pushing. A rebase conflict stops
  it with the branch unchanged, unless the repo's project-map entry names an `onConflict` command (the design system:
  `python3 scripts/ds_register.py regen`, which takes main's copy of generated files, keeps both sides of append-only
  ledgers and reruns the generators); `land` runs it, continues the rebase, and the result takes one full check, except
  in the design system. There (Michael, 2026-11-27, ROC-3768: "Yes - no need to over complicate design system changes -
  it is far too conveluded as is"), a rebase whose only conflicts `regen` settled, or whose only overlap with main is
  in files the branch also changes, takes the static lane plus each lane the branch's own files reach (main's lane map,
  `scripts/ci-land-mode.mjs`), with the landing turn still held, in place of a second full check. A change to how the
  checks run still takes every lane. A site-lane failure this lets through is found by the nightly full check on main.
  Where GitHub requires status checks on main (branch protection or a ruleset), the landed commit needs those checks
  green on it: a clean rebase keeps its pass there only as the next bullet but one says. How `land` takes and lets go of the repo's landing turn, rechecks when main moved, gives up and records its
  timings: `rules/landing-turn.md` (read it when a landing waits for the turn, gives up, rechecks or you land by
  hand).
- Rebase on `origin/main` first, then run the full check once on that exact commit, the one being landed, never on
  earlier commits of the branch (Michael, 2026-11-14, ROC-3240: "All nine, as ranked", approving the pipeline redundancy audit) (the portal's check runs on its pull
  request), then push or open the pull request; a rebase after the full check wastes it. After a rebase that touched
  none of the branch's files, the earlier full-check pass stands once the repo's quick check passes on the rebased
  commit. Crew Console has no quick check and landing runs no local `crew build` (Michael, 2026-11-11, ROC-2943: "Drop
  it (Recommended)"); after a clean rebase its landing checks below stand as the quick check, the earlier green
  `mac-gate` is kept, `land` records it as a green status on the rebased commit, and its push hook accepts land's push
  (Michael, 2026-11-14, ROC-3273: "Yes, option A"). A rebase that touched the branch's files, or a branch with no green
  `mac-gate`, still gets one queued full check on the exact commit. On every Crew landing, `land` also runs SwiftLint on the changed Swift files and Crew's
  `scripts/run-agent-doctor.sh` (its repo checks plus the mac rail, permission catalog and surface map checks) on a clean
  copy of the exact commit it pushes; a failure, or a Mac without SwiftLint, stops the landing (Michael, 2026-11-12,
  ROC-2995: "Yes - as recommended - intend to add all fixes and improvements suggested.").
- The Client Portal's full check is GitHub's "CI passed" in full mode on the pull request's head, with no Mac job: push,
  open the pull request at once and turn on auto-merge.
- Only a repo whose `main` requires a pull request (the Client Portal, rls-demo: `PR_REPOS` in `land.py`) lands by
  pull request, after its own check is green, with auto-merge (rebase method) and Auto-fix on unless the diff touches a
  Tier C path in `rules/risk-tiers.md`. A Tier C path never gets auto-merge. `land` then releases the landing turn and
  watches the pull request until GitHub merges it or a required check fails (ROC-3401): it prints "Landed: <pull
  request> merged" and exits 0, or names each failing job with its link, notes the failure on the ledger (ROC-3253)
  and exits 1, leaving the branch on the pushed commit for a fix; run `land` again after pushing the fix. With auto-merge
  off (Tier C, `--no-auto-merge`) it waits for the checks only and says "Checked, not merged". It never says "Done"
  while CI runs. When the landed diff reaches portal edge functions (`supabase/functions/<name>/` or a `_shared` file
  one imports), it says per function either "deploys automatically after main's CI" (the portal's Deploy workflow does
  it once main's CI is green, after the live-source check; a Tier C one only when every changed file it reaches is
  Tier C and none is the email hold's code, and not while the cleanup quarantine is on, once the portal's selector
  carries ROC-4975) or "waits for Michael's yes", and prints the Deploy command for any held one and for any function with
  no `live/functions/<name>` tag; landing itself never deploys them (`rules/deploys.md`, Michael 2026-11-15, ROC-3406).
  Against a Deploy workflow without the automatic path it says NOT DEPLOYED with each tag's commit instead. A repo whose `main` requires only status checks (the website: `verify`; the design system: `verify` and
  `mac`) fast-forwards main: `land` waits until every required check is green on the exact commit, newest run of each,
  then pushes (ROC-3283). There a clean rebase keeps the earlier pass too (Michael, 2026-11-22, ROC-4585: "Both, clean
  rebase first", after "could we please adapt our landing approach? so we arent so stuck?"; this replaces, for these
  repos, the ROC-3280 line "a rebased commit gets its own full check"): after a rebase that touched none of the
  branch's files, did not change how the check runs (`RECHECK_ALWAYS`, and the repo's own list) and left the patch
  identical (`git patch-id --stable`), the earlier green `verify` and `mac` stand (the design system's quick check is
  its mark-time `scripts/quick.sh`, "What a landing checks" below; land runs no second copy of it). The pass reaches the rebased commit only through
  the repo's own required workflows, run by GitHub Actions on the commit's `land/**` push, never as a status `land`
  posts: main's protection pins each check to GitHub Actions (app 15368), and GitHub counts a pinned check only from
  that app. So a repo takes this rule only when its workflows carry the reuse themselves (the design system's
  `scripts/ci-rebase-reuse.mjs`, ROC-3771) and that script, read from `origin/main`, agrees with `land`; a repo
  without it (the website, for now) and any doubt take a full check on the rebased commit, as before. A reuse round
  is not counted toward the two full checks. The nightly full check on main (`rls-linear main-watch`, see "What a landing checks") is the check after the push. In a repo whose
  workflows trigger on `land/**` (ROC-3735), `land` also pushes
  the commit it checks to a new ref `land/<branch>/<sha12>` (never forced) and its checks run on that push. Not
  workflow_dispatch: main's protection does not count a dispatched run's checks.
- Editing in the worktree while a background `land` runs is safe: a landing never discards an edit or a commit it did
  not make (ROC-2992; twice a stopped landing's `git reset --hard` wiped an hour of edits). It starts only on a clean
  tree, and it never rebases, resolves a conflict or commits in your worktree: the rebase, the repo's `onConflict`
  command (the design system's `ds_register.py regen`) and setting aside an old plugins version bump run in a throwaway copy of
  the branch (ROC-3611). The branch then moves to the result, or back after a stop, only with `git reset --keep`, which
  keeps every uncommitted edit, or refuses and changes nothing. When it gained commits while landing ran, it stays
  where it is. What lands is only what was committed when the check ran. Two cases still stop a landing; land names
  the files, changes nothing, and you commit or finish the edits and land again:
  - main changed a file you have uncommitted edits to, so moving the branch would overwrite them;
  - the repo's quick command runs in your worktree (claude-plugins, Studio Companion, Edit Buddy, Asset Flow, the
    studio board, and Crew Console's `crew quick-land` on a quick landing; the design system has none) and you have uncommitted edits when it would start,
    or edit or commit while it runs. Its result would test your edits, not the commit being landed, so it never
    counts (ROC-3612).
- `land` refuses a branch that puts files back the way they were before a recent main commit, which is what a
  `git reset --soft` onto a newer `origin/main` does (ROC-3305). Rebuild such a branch from `origin/main` with only
  your own changes. An undo that is meant uses `git revert <sha>`, or `rls-linear land --allow-revert "<why>"`, which
  prints the reason with the landing.
- Clear finished worktrees only with `rls-linear worktrees --apply`, or `rls-linear done` for the session's own; both
  check that nothing is lost and nobody uses it. Branches are never deleted, nothing is forced, and each removal is
  archived first (`rls-linear worktrees restore <name>`). `--idle-days <n>` (never under half a day) shortens the 7-day
  idle wait only for a consolidation Michael asked for (2026-11-20, Crew Console cleanup v2: "Can we go ahead and work
  on consolidating the worktrees and branches to main and cleaning from there?"). For a worktree the Claude app leased or pooled, use only
  `git worktree prune`, once its folder is gone, never `git worktree remove`.
- An agent may delete a GitHub branch only when its work is on main (`git cherry origin/main <branch>` lists nothing
  left) or a copy is confirmed on GitHub under an `archive/<date>/` name at the same commit first. `main` is never
  deleted. An `archive/` branch is converted to a tag: it goes only once a tag of the same name holds the same commit
  on GitHub, and new archive copies are tags, not branches (Michael, 2026-11-20, cleanup v2: "Convert to tags
  (Recommended)"). A branch that a dated audit record on main names as its home also goes once a tag under `archive/`
  holds the same commit on GitHub, checked in the run (Michael, 2026-11-20, ROC-4094: "Yes I approve if everything
  was checked by an opus agent and we have a backup if needed"; relayed first as "Yes - as recommended when the tag
  matches the commit"); the session first has an Opus agent verify the list and keeps a backup bundle. The one route is `rls-linear branch-delete <branch>` (a dry run; `--apply`
  deletes), which checks all of this and logs each restore command; the guard refuses every other remote delete,
  including one in a script or a push that names an empty source.
  For many branches at once, `rls-linear branches --apply` (ROC-3586) archives each landed or superseded branch's tip
  at `refs/archive/<date>/<branch>` on GitHub and then deletes it through `branch-delete`; stranded ones are listed only.
  `git cherry` misses work made in a merge commit and a landing later reverted on main, so both commands treat such
  a branch as not landed.

### When to check, push and land
The home of when to push and land; machine/CLAUDE.md, "Checks and waiting", points here (ROC-3935, ROC-5090).
- Commit between landings and push the branch only when something needs it on GitHub: the train, a preview, a
  handoff, another session, or the end of a session that leaves work unlanded. Land once per piece. A branch push runs
  no CI: `rls-linear land` starts the check on the commit it lands (Michael, 2026-11-17: "Yes, stop it", ending CI on
  branch pushes and the push after each step; ROC-3342).
- Land before the piece is finished only when a reader needs the change on main now: `rls-ds`, the Decide site, or a
  session about to branch from `origin/main`. A page republish, a repo copy of an artifact or a status-log line is not
  a piece.
- A session that ends with pushed commits not on main lands them or hands them off (Michael, 2026-11-14, ROC-3342:
  "Yes, all five"). A Stop hook (`scripts/unlanded.py stop`) names commits on a `claude/*` branch that are pushed but
  not on main, once per pushed tip in a session; it never asks for a push. A SessionEnd hook notes the session's branch
  and its commits not on main in `rls-land/unlanded.jsonl`. `rls-linear unlanded` lists pushed `claude/*` branches
  over a day old whose commits main lacks (by `git cherry`), with the session that last left each; the 06:45 repeat
  report includes the list.
- Minor changes land on a secret scan alone, with no test run, in every session (Michael, 2026-11-26: "Yes - and make
  sure this applies to other sessions too - and make sure that it includes other minor changes so we arent running so
  many needless landings"). A minor change is one whose every file is on the minor-change list
  (`config/quick-only-paths.json` in rls-linear): Markdown anywhere outside source, content, test, fixture and resource
  folders, and the pictures, PDFs and plain text under `docs/`. `rls-linear land` rebases it, scans its commits with
  gitleaks and lands it; a repo's commit hook runs only the secret scan for it too. Where a repo has a lane map (the
  design system's Verify decide step) that map decides instead; claude-plugins (its tests read the rules and skills)
  and repos whose main requires status checks keep their checks on the exact commit (ROC-3244).
- A minor change rides along with the piece it belongs to and lands with it. It lands alone only when a reader needs
  it on main now: a rule change other sessions must read, a decision record that closes an issue, or a doc another
  session is about to branch from. A research note, a status line or a page's repo copy waits for the piece. Crew Console,
  Studio Companion and Asset Flow have a landing check scoped to the paths a change touches, with the full suite
  nightly, as Edit Buddy and the kit do (ROC-3245).
- A later step (push hook, pull request, deploy, the push to main) reuses a green status on that exact commit. A step
  that reaches clients, crew or the public reuses only a full check's green (see "What a landing checks").

### The landing train and previews
Michael, 2026-11-23, ROC-4676; 2026-11-24, ROC-4889; 2026-11-25, ROC-5071 (his answers word for word there and in
machine/RULES-HISTORY.md). The train is on for the repos rls-linear `config/train.json` lists (claude-plugins, the
Swift kit, Crew Console, ATLAS and the design system). Every other repo lands each piece as it finishes with
`rls-linear land` and its current landing check, and no preview exists until built; a session or lead holding several
finished branches in one of those repos puts them on one batch branch from the latest `origin/main` (each branch's
commits and trailers kept), lands that once, and on red sends the branch at fault back to its issue as the train does
(Michael, 2026-11-23: "Ban we batch and of these landings together? we have updated rules we adapted you mauy not be
following"). The Client Portal lands its pull requests one at a time, in order, each with its own
whole check, since its "CI passed" and the email and charge guards judge each pull request ("One at a time
(Recommended)"). The Swift kit lands on its quick script checks and its full Mac check runs nightly, and its guard
and rls-gate edits take the quick check too (Michael, 2026-11-23: "Quick + daily full (Recommended)", "No, quick is
enough (Recommended)"; rls-linear `config/quick-landing.json`). A Swift kit release is cut by that nightly full check
when it passes on main's head and plugin files differ from `stable`; a push to kit main cuts no release and runs no
Mac check. A release sooner is one `gh workflow run kit-ci.yml -R RocketLaunchStudio/rls-apple-kit --ref main -f
suite=full` (Michael, 2026-11-27: "Nightly release"). The per-project table is
in the draft linked from ROC-4676.
Quick landing: `rls-linear land` runs the quick check for a repo switched on in rls-linear's
`config/quick-landing.json` (check files: `config/gate-files.json`), and its dry run and report name the check and why.
Where the train is on, plain `rls-linear land` runs the repo's mark-time check (below), pushes the branch and marks that
commit ready on GitHub (`refs/ready/<branch>`), then returns; `--now` lands one branch at once, `--needs-main` marks it
ready and runs the train now. `rls-linear train status|run|freeze|unfreeze|quarantine|measure` reads and drives it from
any Mac: `run` lands only on a signal (`--force` is "asked"), on a stack branch in a throwaway copy through
`rls-linear land`'s own flow, so the check, the Tier C guard and the push are the same. Tier C never rides it
(`rls-linear land --now --approved` with Michael's yes). A fast-forward repo (Crew Console, the website) does not read
an independent review yet, so Tier C code there lands only on his yes until a record a session cannot forge exists
(ROC-5011; `rules/risk-tiers.md`, "Tier C code changes"). A freeze is `rls-linear train freeze --reason "..." --until 8h`.
The clock moves to the studio's always-on check Mac, as a plain launchd agent that takes no check slot (Michael,
2026-11-24, ROC-4889; his words in machine/RULES-HISTORY.md). The clock is `rls-linear train tick` every 30 minutes.
The check Mac's runs as its `agent` account (LaunchDaemon `com.rocketlaunchstudio.train.agent`, installed and checked
by `machine/train_clock.py`, ROC-4905); the laptop's (rls-linear `config/com.rocketlaunchstudio.train.plist`) stays
until the check Mac's has run a day (`train_clock.py retire-laptop`). Each repo's `refs/train/clock` (`rls-linear train clock`)
names the one Mac whose sweeper drives it, so two clocks never sweep one repo; a run on another Mac stands aside while
`refs/train/running/<mac>` says a run of that repo (or branch) is going there. Each run is recorded on
the relay (`/health`, `train`; "The relay - though its health needs to be checked to make sure it works"; "Heartbeat +
fallback (Recommended)"); no run for an hour shows one line on Michael's next prompt and in the 06:45 report, and
any session may run `rls-linear train run --force` in the repo meanwhile; while the clock is down, marking a branch
ready starts the train for it at once.
The train clears its own branches (ROC-5324): after a run it deletes its `train/*` stack and the `land/<stack>/*` CI
refs, `rls-linear land` deletes the `land/<branch>/<sha>` refs it pushed once main holds them, and `train tick` runs
`train tidy-refs` every two hours, which deletes `land/*` and `train/*` branches already on main and archives (to
`refs/archive/<day>/`) then deletes those older than a day. Every delete goes through `branch_delete` with its log and
restore command. A landing leaves `refs/train/landed/<branch>` for seven days, so `rls-linear train wait --branch <b>`
(the checks skill, "Watch what you wait on") can tell landed from sent back for a reader who needs it on main.

#### What a landing checks
Michael, 2026-11-25, ROC-5071: "Almost nothing needs the full check - the only thing that really needs the full check
would be the ending". One home for which check a change takes; the checks skill says how to run and watch one, and each
repo's AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md names its commands and lane map.
- Working (branch commits, Debug builds, previews, builds for Michael's own devices): the build only.
- Marking ready: `rls-linear land` rebases the branch on origin/main in a throwaway copy, refuses it, naming the files,
  when it conflicts or undoes main's work, and runs the repo's mark-time check once on a clean copy of the rebased
  commit on the session's own Mac (config/train.json `markCheck`: the design system's `scripts/quick.sh`;
  claude-plugins' stale-copy, skill-budget and `plugin validate --strict` steps; the Swift kit's shellcheck and
  validate steps; ROC-5341). A failure
  leaves the branch unmarked and costs no GitHub run. No check runs on GitHub for a branch alone before it is marked
  ready (Michael, 2026-11-25: "Drop now - but note to check and see if it actually is improved after we try a few").
  After the first 10 landings on this flow, `rls-linear train measure <repo>` compares ready-to-main time, runner
  minutes and send-backs with `docs/landing-checks/measurements-2026-11-25.md`, and the result goes on ROC-5071.
- Landing: one check per batch, scoped by the paths the batch changes. Where a repo has a lane map (the design system's
  Verify decide step, always read from origin/main), the batch runs the static lane plus each lane its paths reach,
  every lane for a path the map does not know, and every lane for a change to how the checks run. Elsewhere the train's
  check is the repo's quick check, except a change to the checks themselves, which takes the full check. The train runs
  no laptop copy of a check the batch's own run repeats: in the design system no quick check on the stack and no
  landing quick.sh, since the static lane runs the same checks on the exact commit main requires. Client Portal and the
  website, whose landings go live ("Full check on landing (Recommended)"), and claude-plugins and linear-relay, which
  reach every session ("Whole check on landing (Recommended)"), take their whole check on every landing: there the
  landing is the ending.
- The ending: the full check runs only there (Michael, 2026-11-25, ROC-5071: "Only at the ending (Recommended)"),
  never after a landing. Nightly, on each quick-landing repo's main, started by the relay, not GitHub's schedule
  (`rls-linear main-watch <repo>`, which skips a main that has not moved since its last green); before a web kit
  release (the Swift kit releases from its nightly full check, above) and anything else that reaches clients, crew or
  the public (a production deploy or promotion, TestFlight
  beyond Michael's own group, the App Store, a production migration), green on that exact commit; for a change to how
  the checks run, before it lands; and on request at a project's close (`rls-linear main-watch <repo>` by hand). A red
  one files one issue, or counts on the open one, naming the landings since the last green; it pauses nothing, is
  fixed next, and blocks the next release until green ("File and fix, no pause (Recommended)").
- When a repo's train runs (Michael, 2026-11-24, ROC-4889: "Instead of it being a train that arbitratily waits - it
  should go on ready, with perhaps a process that checks other claude sessions - without interrupting them too much in
  a way that would derail them - to assess if theres anything in the next few minutes it can batch - if not, then it
  goes as ready"; replacing 2026-11-23 "Within 30 minutes (Recommended)"): marking a branch ready starts its repo's
  train. It first looks, without messaging any session, for another branch in that repo about to be ready in the next
  few minutes, and waits for it only then, at most 3 minutes (config/train.json `holdMinutes`; "Up to 3 minutes
  (Recommended)"; kept at 3 on 2026-11-25, ROC-5071, since time to main wins: "Time to main (Recommended)"); it keeps
  landing until nothing is ready. A timer stays as a sweeper. At most one run and one waiting run per repo; a mark made while one
  waits starts nothing (ROC-4948). It does not run while a freeze is on. Every repo rides it ("Every
  repo (Recommended)"); `--now` lands one branch at once for an urgent fix or a reader.
- Own check, then land, in the design system (Michael, 2026-11-25, about 22:30 EST, ROC-5071: "Yes, prove then build",
  to "Switch the design system to own-check-then-land, and run the four proofs first?"; it replaces, for the design
  system, the batch above and his "Drop now" of a branch's own check). A repo with `"each": true` in config/train.json
  lands every ready branch alone, as soon as it is marked, in its own `rls-linear train run --branch` process beside any
  other: no batch, no look-ahead hold, no wait behind a running train. Its check is that branch's own scoped check on
  the exact commit; the landing turn still serializes pushes to main, and a clean rebase keeps the pass. Why (the
  proofs, 2026-11-18 to 25): the batch train took a median 78 and a mean 117 minutes from ready to main, mostly queued
  behind the running train, while the same 29 branches replayed one by one take a median 10.5 and a mean 11.8; 78% of
  failures belonged to one branch alone; of 677 re-checks after main moved, 8 failed and none was a real clash; and of
  13 red runs re-run on the same commit, 5 passed. Every other train repo follows, one at a time (next bullet).
- Retiring the batch machinery (Michael, 2026-11-26, ROC-5124; his answers on the list in
  `docs/landing-checks/mechanisms-2026-11-26.md`). Once each branch lands alone these go: batching and halving, with
  the stack's cheap pre-check and the split by check level ("Batching and halving (Recommended)"); the look-ahead hold
  ("3-minute look-ahead hold (Recommended)"); the 24-hour no-recheck of a red tree and the train's `--again` on ready
  marks ("24-hour no-recheck and --again"; "Drop it on the train (Recommended)": a re-marked commit is simply checked
  again, and `land --again` stays for landings outside the train); lane probes on main ("Lane probes on main"); the
  mark-time check ("Mark-time check (Recommended)"); the laptop clock, once the always-on Mac's clock runs ("Laptop
  train clock (Recommended)", ROC-4905); and, with or after ROC-5125, the main-red pause and the confirmed-red hold
  ("Main-red pause"; "Pause goes, guard stays (Recommended)"): nobody is sent back for a failure main's own full check
  also has, but no ready branch waits for main. The flaky-test quarantine stays. Every train repo moves to `"each":
  true`, one at a time (the Swift kit, then Crew Console and ATLAS, then claude-plugins), each only after the session
  checks and posts on ROC-5124 that the repo is set up for it: its landing check, its lane map or quick-landing config,
  and the statuses main requires ("Every repo, while checking to make sure they're primed to use the correct landing
  process"). Each removal takes effect when its code lands, starting after the design system's first 10 landings since
  422d87a02593 are measured (ROC-5071); until then the tools work as the bullets around this one say.
- One check on the ready branches together; on red, it finds the branch at fault and the rest land ("One check, then
  find culprit (Recommended)", 2026-11-23). It reads the failing lanes and tests from the log (the first failing test,
  never a passing test whose name holds the word "error"), and the branches whose files the failure names are the
  suspects; the names of a check's own runner scripts are no evidence (config/train.json `runnerFiles`). With
  suspects it checks the others first; with none it gives the batch one named re-run (Flaky tests, below) and, where
  the repo takes a lane probe (config/train.json `laneProbe`), runs the failed lanes on main alone beside it: when main
  fails the same tests the failure is main's, nobody is halved or sent back, main's full check starts and the train
  pauses until main moves. Otherwise it halves, never re-checking a tree already known to fail nor re-running a failure
  already confirmed in the round. Re-running failed lanes on each suspect alone, side by side, waits for the
  10-landing measurement (Michael, 2026-11-25, ROC-5071: "minimum - then measure - and consider if the method we are
  working towards is really in our best interest"). Branches that need different checks are split by check level, so a light branch never waits on a
  heavy neighbour's slow check (Michael, 2026-11-24, ROC-4889: "Split by check level (Recommended)", "with a smarter
  approach, research ways we can make the appraoch quicker and based on more relevant insight"). The branch at fault
  goes back to its issue, set to Todo with the error, for the next free session or the dispatcher ("Back to its issue
  (Recommended)").
- Flaky tests (Michael, 2026-11-25, ROC-5071: "Yeah quarantine - and assess if what we are resting is flawed and if
  that test can be disregarded - bypassing that flaky error. Also - we must implement a method that self corrects for
  things like this - that many sessions shouldnt be sent back for a flaky error like that, they should adapt so we dont
  get ourselves stuck wasting minutes and time"). A red check whose failure names no branch in the batch and is not
  main's own gets one named re-run of its failed jobs on the same commit ("one named re-run: <tests>"). If that passes,
  the batch lands and the test is a flake: the train quarantines it with an issue and a 7-day expiry, and notes it on
  the failure ledger; the issue asks whether the test is flawed and can be dropped or rewritten. A quarantined test
  still runs on every landing and reports, but cannot send work back; the nightly full check and every release run it
  strictly. A test the round's re-run confirmed is not re-run again in the round. The list is `refs/train/quarantine`
  on the repo, written only by the train or by hand (`rls-linear train quarantine` lists, adds and removes; adding
  again renews the 7 days; never a whole lane or a whole test file); the design system's Verify reads it (main's copy
  of `scripts/verify_quarantine.mjs`). A failure that names no test (only a lane or the environment) on two unrelated
  branches still pauses the repo's train until main moves.
- When main itself is red (ROC-4944, ROC-4953) (Michael, 2026-11-24, ROC-4889: "Write it (Recommended)"). A repo whose full check posts a commit status on main (config/train.json
  `fullCheckStatus`; the design system's `full-check`) is judged by that status. A red seen once is run again first and
  landings go on meanwhile; a red on two commits since the last green, or twice on one commit, is confirmed. While it
  is confirmed, nobody is sent back for a failure main also has, and only needs-main branches and branches touching
  what it fails on land, each alone and ahead of any halving; every other ready branch waits and stays ready. The
  landing of main's fix (the main-fix holder's branch, or a needs-main mark) starts main's full check again; no other
  landing does, and none starts one while a session holds main's fix (ROC-5071).
- One fixer for a red main (ROC-4951) (Michael, 2026-11-24, ROC-4889: "Write it (Recommended)"). Before building anything for a red main, run `rls-linear main-fix show`. If a
  session holds main's fix, reach it on its issue and build nothing for main's red unless it hands the fix over. If
  nobody does, take it first with `rls-linear main-fix claim --issue ROC-<n>` (a `land --needs-main` while main is red
  takes it for the branch's issue by itself). While another session holds it, `land` refuses a needs-main mark,
  `--now`, and a branch touching what main's failure names; `--not-main-fix "<why>"` is only for a branch that is not a
  fix for main. The claim is `refs/train/main-fix` on GitHub, so every Mac, subagent and cloud session obeys it; a hold
  sent only by message does not count. It clears when main's full check is green on a newer main, and goes stale 3
  hours after its holder last marked ready, landed or claimed.
- Who owns a piece after it is marked ready (Michael, 2026-11-24, ROC-4889 and ROC-4901): marking ready releases the
  claim, and a send-back always sets the issue to Todo with the error and tells the session that marked it, except a
  parent issue held by another live session ("Release and Todo (Recommended)", replacing the agent-made 2026-11-24 rule
  that a claim under a day old keeps the state). The session proves each Done-when line when it marks ready, or names
  what waits on a date or a measurement, and the train closes the issue at landing when that proof covers every line
  and its own check passed, never for Risk C ("Train closes on proof (Recommended)"). At landing the train also sets
  every other state itself: Blocked with a `Waiting on:` line for a date or measurement, Todo for work left; nothing
  waits on Michael alone ("Train sets it - nothing should wait on me exclusively. Allow agents to fully control that
  process, I never really open the items myself in linear."). Built 2026-11-25 (ROC-4901, ROC-4867,
  ROC-4869): `rls-linear land --proof "1=...; 2=landing" --waiting-on "3: <what>"` stores the proof on the ready mark,
  which moves the issue to In Review and releases the claim; the train closes, blocks or sets Todo at landing and sends
  a send-back to Todo addressed to the session on the mark; a sent-back commit is marked again only with `--again
  "<why>"` until that refusal is removed (Michael, 2026-11-26: "Drop it on the train (Recommended)"; bullet above);
  `rls-linear train status` and the morning report list send-backs not on main (the linear skill's
  `references/finish-and-git.md`). A mark with no proof lands to Todo for the next session to prove.
- How a send-back reaches a session (ROC-5341; Michael, 2026-11-27: "Yes - with limits"). The train first retries a
  branch that conflicts only with an earlier branch of its own stack and applies to main alone, on the new main, once.
  A send-back is left for the session on the ready mark, which hears it at its next prompt or turn end. The train wakes
  that session (`claude --bg --resume`) only when it ran on this laptop, ended within 24 hours and is not still open,
  at most once per send-back and 6 times a day, and only when the load guard would let a session start; otherwise the
  send-back is one line on Michael's next prompt. Each send-back gets a class from its first error; a class seen on a
  second branch gets one fix issue (marked `Send-back class:`), later hits comment on it and pass its `Try next:`
  line to the session, a hit after its fix reopens it, and a fix that held 7 days is said once.
  `rls-linear train classes [repo] --apply` classes the send-backs already logged. Every send-back and wake decision
  is a row in train.jsonl (`kind: "branch"` with `signature` and `fixIssue`; `kind: "wake"`), read by the failure
  board.
- A freeze is turned on by the session leading the risky step, with one command naming the repo, the reason and an
  end time; it shows on the issue and in the morning report and lifts at the end time unless renewed. Michael can
  also say "freeze <repo>" in chat ("The leading session (Recommended)").
- RLS Demo is an internal tool only, to be folded into the design system; its landing takes much quicker checks than
  today's full gate on every pull request (Michael, 2026-11-24, ROC-4889: "Undeerstand also that is is exclusively an
  internal tool - so that it can go through much quicker checks"). It lands on its own train now, without a pull
  request, on a quick check (static checks, a Debug build of both apps, tests of the packages a change touches); its
  full gate and launch check run nightly and before TestFlight builds, and main stops requiring the gate ("Quick land,
  full nightly (Recommended)", "Own train now (Recommended)"). After the fold it rides the design system's train in
  its own lane. Until this is built, its current gate stays.
- Crew Console's quick check is lint, the agent doctor and a Debug build of only the targets a change touches;
  backend and docs changes build nothing ("Build what it touches (Recommended)").
- A finishing session marks its branch ready and never waits ("Should depend on the nature of the agent, and if its a
  leader or a subagent. Whether it hands off, continues and moves on, spawns another agent, updates linear. But it
  shouldnt just wait"; 2026-11-24, ROC-4889: "Yes, never wait (Recommended)"): a subagent reports to its lead with its
  branch and stops; a lead continues with a direct follow-on or hands off; an unattended run hands off and may start its successor.
  A landing, or the train where a repo's train is on, posts each branch's result, red or green, on its issue and to
  anyone waiting on it, and a red result sends the branch back there. A cloud session marks nothing ready (machine
  CLAUDE.md, "Work list").
- Previews, started on demand by an agent or Michael, private behind Cloudflare Access, the build only ("Branch previews
  (Recommended)", "Build only", "Agent or you, on demand (Recommended)"). Web sites (Client Portal, website, the
  design system doc site, docs): one preview per branch, brought up to date with main first, plus one combined preview
  of main and every open branch that merges cleanly, naming each branch left out and its conflict ("Both kinds
  (Recommended)"). Portal previews run the Worker only, on the production database with the demo client and admin
  screens ("Production, demo client only"; "Admin too"), with email, payments and outbound calls blocked, deletes and
  bulk changes refused outside the demo client ("Block deletes outside demo (Recommended)"); edge function and schema
  changes are not previewed. Apple apps: a just-Michael TestFlight or direct install from any branch ("Any branch,
  build only (Recommended)"; Crew Console's `dev-*` lane needs Michael's Xcode Cloud step, ROC-1080). Edit Buddy keeps
  its landing check before an install over his real app; the Pi is previewed on a simulated Pi on the Mac and its
  `make deploy` keeps `make test`; claude-plugins and linear-relay have no preview ("Approve, Edit Buddy keeps gate
  (Recommended)"; "All projects should allow for a fast lane preview/staging capability").

## Deploys and Cloudflare
- Deploy only through the repo's own deploy script or CI workflow, never by calling a deploy tool directly or skipping
  its checks. This covers publishing a Worker or Pages build.
- Client Portal edge functions deploy automatically after a green CI run on main, through the Deploy workflow, which
  keeps its live-source check. A function counts as changed when its folder, or a `_shared` file it imports directly
  or through other shared files, changed since the commit in its `live/functions/<name>` tag. A Tier C function
  deploys after its landing only when every changed file it reaches is itself a Tier C path, none is the email hold's
  code, the cleanup quarantine is lifted (mode `lifted`; `on` and `lifting` hold it), and every pull request that
  landed one of its changes since its tag carries a passing review record or Michael's yes for the patch it landed,
  posted after that rule landed on main (a yes given when it meant landing only never deploys); otherwise it waits for
  Michael's yes and a manual `target=functions` run (Michael, 2026-11-24, ROC-4975: "I land them, you approve acts
  (Recommended)", narrowed by that change's independent reviews, B1, M1 and review 2's item 3; it supersedes 2026-11-15's "Yes, non-Tier C only", ROC-3406;
  `rules/risk-tiers.md`, "Tier C code changes"). The run summary of each automatic run lists what it deployed and
  what waits; a red "Edge functions not deployed" job means a live-source mismatch, a failed deploy or changes it
  could not work out, and a function with no tag is listed but never deployed automatically (portal
  `scripts/deploy/select-functions.mjs`). Until that selector carries ROC-4975 on the portal's main, every Tier C
  function waits for a manual `target=functions` run.
- The Client Portal Worker goes live a few times a day, not on every merge (Michael, 2026-11-17: "Batch a few times
  a day (Recommended)", ROC-3800). A green CI run on main deploys changed edge functions as above and
  uploads the Worker as a version tagged with its commit, not live; the Deploy workflow's schedule (three off-the-hour
  times a day, which GitHub starts on or after that time) puts the newest upload on main live with `wrangler versions
  deploy`, or skips when it already is (portal `scripts/deploy/pick-worker-version.mjs`). A fix that cannot wait runs
  the Deploy workflow by hand: `target=promote` (the newest upload, in seconds) or `target=worker` (build and deploy
  now). Check production after the promotion that carries your change, not after the merge. A portal migration that
  removes or renames something waits until the Worker code that stops using it is live (portal
  `docs/runbooks/github-deploy.md`, "Batched Worker deploys").
- Use the `cloudflare` plugin server
  (search, docs, execute, whoami) for the account and Wrangler inside a repo; `rls-linear parity` checks that the plugin
  is on. Do not rely on a claude.ai Cloudflare connector, which belongs to one account. If a session has no `cloudflare`
  plugin server, say so and use Wrangler.
- Other Cloudflare steps follow `rules/risk-tiers.md`. Paid plans,
  raised limits and permanently deleting production data (a D1 database, KV namespace, R2 bucket or its objects) are
  Risk C: ask Michael in chat first.

### Merges that deploy
Moved word for word from machine/CLAUDE.md, "Git: several sessions share each repo" (ROC-3935).
- A green Risk A or B merge in the portal or website deploys through the repo's own deploy workflow without asking; then
  check production. The portal's Worker goes live in batches: the merge uploads it and the Deploy workflow's schedule
  puts it live a few times a day (`rules/deploys.md`).

## Changing the rules: the procedure
- When Michael changes a rule in chat, write it into its file (plugin, CLAUDE.md or skill) before acting on it, add his
  exact words and the date to `machine/RULES-HISTORY.md` for a rule in machine/CLAUDE.md, in the files holding text moved out of it
  (`rules/landing.md`, `landing-turn.md`, `deploys.md`, `folders.md`, `changing-the-rules.md`, `models.md`), in the macs skill
  or in the linear skill's `references/handing-off.md`, record his exact words on every issue it decides with `rls-linear comment`,
  and say which sessions must restart: a session keeps the text it loaded at start.
- Agents never make a rule on their own conclusion. His words in chat apply at once. To propose a new or changed rule,
  ask him in chat right then with the proposed text, the file, why, and your recommendation, so he can approve it at
  once. Without his yes nothing is written.
- In a session he is not in, file the proposal on Linear titled "Proposed rule: ..." (Owner Michael, Ask Product call)
  for the weekly rules review with Monday planning.
- Existing rules are audited in rounds of up to 30, those without a quote of his first.
- Dated planning notes (`*_2026-*.md`, `SPEC.md`) are history and evidence, not rules. Rules live in the machine-wide CLAUDE.md and the files it cites, in each
  repo's files and in the plugins.
- Cloud sessions and other AI tools never see the machine-wide CLAUDE.md or `~/.claude`: they read the repo's
  `AGENTS.md` and the public live file
  `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RocketLaunchStudio/studio-rules/main/STUDIO_RULES.md`, generated from these rules
  by the rls-linear plugin's `scripts/studio_rules.py`. Each repo fetches it at session start, through its cloud hook or
  its `AGENTS.md`. A repo's `STUDIO_RULES.md` is only a backup for when the live file cannot be fetched; its being
  behind is not a failure.

## Models: the full rule
- Pick each agent's model for the job, not the topic, and give the reason in the brief.
- Haiku: lookups and sweeps, such as finding the files that import a module, checking links or listing issues.
- Sonnet: work built from something already decided (an approved template, drawing, spec or rule set) that a check or
  screenshot verifies: ports, screens from an approved design, copy edits, mechanical refactors.
- Opus: planning, briefs, review, risky changes, design inside an existing system, root-cause investigations and
  architecture calls.
- Fable is off by default for now because of cost. Use it only when the person asks, or when Opus has already tried the
  same job and fallen short; say which in the brief. Being new, ambiguous, long or design work is not by itself a
  reason.
- Subagents never inherit the parent's model. Every Agent call sets `model`, its brief has a line "Model: <name>,
  because <reason>", and a Workflow script names `model` on every agent call. A model above the one an agent's own file
  pins names that pin in the Model line and says why. A fork runs on the parent's model, so a Fable session never forks
  or starts Fable subagents; it hands that work to Sonnet or Opus. The report says which model each agent ran on. The
  rls-linear Agent hook refuses a call that breaks any of these, except the pin: a model above the agent file's pin
  whose Model line does not name it goes through with a warning, logged in `~/.local/state/rls/model-pin-warnings.jsonl`
  (Michael, 2026-11-14: "Turn the refusal into a warning").
- Sessions started from another session (`start_session`, user_asked or own_initiative) name `model` and `effort`, with
  the reason in the brief. Effort is low for waiting on a check and landing, medium for most building and fixing, high
  only for planning, review or a risky change. When a session's risky part is done and only landing is left, lower its
  effort with `set_session_effort`; move it to a cheaper model with `set_session_model` only when 15 or more requests
  are likely to remain. A model switch rewrites the whole prompt cache at the new model's price (about $0.57 at 150k
  context, Opus to Sonnet) and pays back after about 12 to 14 requests; of 10 such switches in the 14 days to
  2026-11-19, 4 lost money (Michael, 2026-11-19: "Yes, as recommended"). Forks, offers, proposal starts, presets and cloud starts are
  exempt. The same hook refuses a call without both.
- Which work goes where, and how it is checked (Michael, 2026-11-18, ROC-3917: "Yes, land all three", after asking
  that the rule "detail ... which sessions are exceptions and not run on opus - or when or when not to check the work
  of a sonnet agent based on the type of work it performs rather than automatically assuming accuracy"; evidence:
  `docs/token-spend/trial-2026-11.md` in claude-plugins). The bullets below are that rule.
- Stays on Opus: the lead session (it plans, writes briefs, decides and checks what agents return); Risk C and D work
  and anything touching money, sign-in, client data or production data; changes to shared gates, guards, CI, hooks and
  rules files; root-cause work where the cause is not yet known; design judgement whose verdict decides what Michael
  is shown, and the independent registrar; and review, checking claims against a source, and audits that a decision,
  a landing or a report to Michael rests on. In the 2026-11 trial Sonnet found 80% of confirmed review findings, 61%
  of check findings and 64% of audit findings against a bar of 90%, and passed risky items Opus caught.
- Goes to Sonnet: work built from something already decided that a command, test or screenshot proves; mechanical
  edits and ports; and lookups and sweeps where every claim comes back with its evidence and a missed item costs
  little because a later step or check would catch it. Haiku for the simplest of these. Sonnet's shortfall in the
  trial was missed findings (53 of 158), not wrong ones (3 of 105), so work that must be complete is not Sonnet's.
- Checking a Sonnet agent depends on the kind of work; its accuracy is never assumed:
  - proved by a command (tests, a check, a screenshot): the lead runs it or reads its result on that commit. No
    reviewer is needed;
  - fact finding (a lookup or sweep): every claim carries its evidence (file and line, command output, or URL and
    quote). The lead checks at least 3 claims or 1 in 5, and every claim a hard-to-undo step rests on. One wrong
    claim: check them all or rerun on Opus. A spot check cannot show what was left out;
  - judgement (a review verdict, design compliance, a suspected cause): stays on Opus. If a Sonnet agent returns one
    anyway it is a lead, not a verdict: Opus confirms each finding before anyone acts, and "nothing found" or "this is
    safe" on risky work is not a pass;
  - code edits: Risk A, the repo's check; Risk B, the check plus the lead reads the diff.
- When a Sonnet agent falls short (it fails its check twice, says it is unsure, contradicts itself, or a spot check
  finds a wrong claim), rerun the job on Opus and pass along what the first attempt found. Never a third Sonnet try.
  The lead names the escalation in its report. A kind of work that escalates more than 1 time in 5 goes back to Opus
  by default, and a kind of work kept on Opus moves to Sonnet only through a new measured trial, never a session's
  own judgement.
- Effort for subagents: every Agent call passes `effort`, whatever its model, and so does every agent() call in a
  Workflow script. A line in the brief does not set it: without the parameter the agent runs at its usual effort,
  which for Opus subagents was high on 90% of requests in the week to 2026-11-24
  (`docs/token-spend/effort-2026-11.md`). The rls-linear Agent hook refuses a call that passes none, except a fork, a
  web-fetch agent or an agent whose own file pins `effort:` (Michael, 2026-11-24, ROC-5013: "Yes, write it
  (Recommended)"). Low for lookups and sweeps; medium for work from a decided spec; high for bug fixes and anything
  with edge cases. Opus review agents run at medium; check and audit agents stay at high until a trial covers them. A
  review that a decision on money, email, sign-in, client data, gates or hooks rests on gets two independent Opus
  reviewers at medium instead of one at high, and the lead merges their findings (Michael, 2026-11-25, ROC-5026: "Yes,
  write it (Recommended)"; trial: `docs/token-spend/trial-review-effort-2026-11.md`, medium found 81% of confirmed
  findings against 63% at high, at 65% of the cost). `max` is not used without a measured reason. High wrote about 10%
  more output per request than medium in a week of transcripts, roughly 2% more cost: it buys care, it is not a
  savings lever.
